questions.question: A static game can be described by its normal form. What extra information does an extensive-form description of a game add to the normal form?
options: The payoffs of every player at every profile of pure strategies.
Common knowledge of the game, which the normal form does not assume.
The order of moves and what each player has observed when she moves.
The list of each player's pure strategies, which the normal form omits.

questions.question: In the game tree of an extensive-form game, why does each terminal node correspond to exactly one complete play of the game?
options: Every decision node offers exactly two actions, so each terminal node is reached by one choice per mover.
Every node except the root has exactly one immediate predecessor, so its path from the root is unique.
Each player moves exactly once on every path, so the sequence of movers is the same for every play.
Different terminal nodes must carry different payoff vectors, so a payoff vector identifies the play.

questions.question: In an extensive-form game, each player's decision nodes are partitioned into information sets. When does the game have perfect information?
options: When every player knows the payoff functions of all the other players.
When the game contains no move by Nature at any of its decision nodes.
When the whole structure of the game is common knowledge among the players.
When every information set of every player is a single decision node.

questions.question: Some extensive-form games include moves by Nature, for example a random draw of the weather. How is such a move represented in the game?
options: By an extra player with her own payoffs, who chooses the action that gives her the highest payoff.
By a node at which all players move at once, so that nobody observes the outcome of the draw.
By a node whose probabilities each player chooses as part of her own strategy in the game.
By a decision node of Nature, which picks among its actions with a fixed probability distribution.

questions.question: Firm 1 sets its price on Monday. Firm 2 sets its price on Wednesday without having learned firm 1's price. How is firm 2's move represented in the extensive form?
options: Firm 2 has a singleton information set after each price of firm 1, because it moves later.
The game cannot be drawn as a tree, because the two firms in effect choose simultaneously.
Firm 2's nodes after the different prices of firm 1 all lie in one information set.
Firm 2 must be drawn at the root, because it is the firm that lacks information when moving.

questions.question: In an extensive-form game, player 1 first chooses one of three actions; after each of them player 2 chooses one of two actions, and then the game ends. How many decision nodes and how many terminal nodes does the game tree have?
options: $4$ decision nodes and $6$ terminal nodes.
$2$ decision nodes and $6$ terminal nodes.
$3$ decision nodes and $6$ terminal nodes.
$4$ decision nodes and $5$ terminal nodes.

questions.question: In the entry game, entrant $E$ chooses Out, giving payoffs $(0,2)$ to $(E,I)$, or In; after In, incumbent $I$ chooses Accommodate, $(1,1)$, or Fight, $(-1,-1)$. In the normal form, the entrant chooses Out or In and the incumbent chooses Accommodate or Fight. Which payoff pair belongs in the cell (Out, Fight)?

Player 1 chooses $O$ or $F$; player 2 observes this and chooses $O$ or $F$. Payoffs: $(O,O)\mapsto(2,1)$, $(F,F)\mapsto(1,2)$, and $(0,0)$ after a mismatch. The game is converted to its normal form, with player 1's pure strategies as rows and player 2's as columns. What are the dimensions of the payoff table?
options: $2$ rows and $2$ columns.
$4$ rows and $4$ columns.
$4$ rows and $2$ columns.
$2$ rows and $4$ columns.

questions.question: Player 1 moves first. Player 2 observes player 1's move and then moves. Player 3 then moves, having observed player 1's move but not player 2's. Does this extensive-form game have perfect or imperfect information?
options: Imperfect: player 3 cannot tell apart nodes that differ only in player 2's move.
Perfect: player 3 observes the first move, and that is enough for perfect information.
Perfect: player 2 observes player 1, so every move in the game is observed by someone.
Imperfect: player 2 does not observe player 3's later move before she has to choose.

questions.question: Nature first chooses state $G$ with probability $0.3$ or state $B$ with probability $0.7$. Player 1 then chooses Invest or Wait without observing the state. Invest pays her $10$ in $G$ and $-2$ in $B$; Wait pays $0$. What is her expected payoff from Invest?
An extensive-form game requires the same set of actions to be available at every node of an information set. Why is this requirement needed?
options: Otherwise the game might fail to have a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in its normal form.
Otherwise the actions on offer would reveal to the mover which node she is at.
Otherwise the terminal nodes below different nodes of the set could carry different payoffs.
Otherwise the game would have perfect information, since every node would be a singleton.

questions.question: Nature first draws the weather, and both players observe it. Player 1 then moves, and player 2 observes player 1's move before moving. Does this extensive-form game have perfect information?
options: Yes: every information set is a singleton, since all moves are observed.
No: any move by Nature makes the information imperfect, whether or not it is observed.
No: the players do not know the weather before the game starts, so information is imperfect.
Yes, but only if Nature chooses each type of weather with the same probability.

questions.question: In the entry game, entrant $E$ chooses Out, giving payoffs $(0,2)$ to $(E,I)$, or In; after In, incumbent $I$ chooses Accommodate, $(1,1)$, or Fight, $(-1,-1)$. The profile (Out, Fight) is a Nash equilibrium of the normal form. Why can the normal form not show that the threat to fight is never tested?
options: Because (Out, Fight) is not in fact a Nash equilibrium of the normal form of this game.
Because the normal form gives the incumbent fewer strategies than she has in the tree.
Because Nash equilibria of the tree are defined differently from those of the normal form.
Against Out she gets $2$ in both columns, and the table hides that she moves only after In.

questions.question: In the entry game, entrant $E$ chooses Out, giving payoffs $(0,2)$ to $(E,I)$, or In; after In, incumbent $I$ chooses Accommodate, $(1,1)$, or Fight, $(-1,-1)$. Which list gives exactly the pure-strategy Nash equilibria of this game, found from its $2\times2$ normal form?
options: (In, Accommodate) only.
(In, Accommodate) and (Out, Fight).
(Out, Accommodate) and (Out, Fight).
(In, Accommodate), (Out, Accommodate) and (Out, Fight).

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $O$ or $F$; player 2 observes this and chooses $O$ or $F$. Payoffs: $(O,O)\mapsto(2,1)$, $(F,F)\mapsto(1,2)$, and $(0,0)$ after a mismatch. Player 2's pure strategies are written (reply to $O$, reply to $F$). Which play and payoffs does the profile in which player 1 plays $F$ and player 2 plays $(F,O)$ produce?
options: Player 1 plays $F$, then player 2 plays $O$; payoffs $(0,0)$.
Player 1 plays $F$, then player 2 plays $F$; payoffs $(1,2)$.
Player 1 plays $F$, then player 2 plays $O$; payoffs $(1,2)$.
No single play: player 2 waits to see $F$ before her plan applies.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $A$, $B$ or $C$. Player 2 learns only whether $A$ was chosen: her nodes after $B$ and after $C$ form one information set, and her node after $A$ is a singleton. At each information set she chooses $x$ or $y$. How many pure strategies does player 2 have?

In the entry game, entrant $E$ chooses Out, giving payoffs $(0,2)$ to $(E,I)$, or In; after In, incumbent $I$ chooses Accommodate, $(1,1)$, or Fight, $(-1,-1)$. Game Y has the same players, actions and payoffs, but the incumbent chooses Accommodate or Fight without observing whether the entrant entered. Which statement comparing the entry game and Y is correct?
options: Y has a different normal form, because the incumbent cannot condition her action on entry.
The incumbent has $4$ strategies in the entry game but $2$ in Y, so the normal forms differ.
(Out, Fight) is a Nash equilibrium of Y but not of the entry game, since there she moves later.
Both have the same $2\times2$ normal form, hence the same Nash equilibria (In, A) and (Out, F).

questions.question: To save space, a modeller draws the plays ($L$, then $a$) and ($R$, then $b$) as arrows into one and the same terminal node $z$ carrying payoff vector $v(z)$. Why is this not a valid extensive-form game?
options: It is valid as long as both plays give the same payoff vector, because only $v(z)$ matters.
It is valid as long as the two final moves are made by different players at their nodes.
Then $z$ has two immediate predecessors, so it no longer marks a unique play.
It is invalid because $z$ would then lie in two information sets, one for each incoming play.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $L$ or $R$. Player 2, without observing this, chooses $l$ or $r$. Player 1 then observes player 2's choice, remembers her own, and chooses $x$ or $y$. How many pure strategies does player 1 have?

Player 1 chooses Stop, ending the game with payoffs $(1,0)$, or Continue. Player 2 then chooses Stop, $(0,2)$, or Continue. Player 1 then chooses Stop, $(3,1)$, or Continue, $(2,4)$. All moves are observed. How many pure-strategy Nash equilibria does the normal form have?
